notes: Committal appeal; contempt finding upheld but suspended sentence quashed for sentencing error.

enrichment.short_title: M (Children): committal appeal over late return of child to mother
key_facts: Mr M appealed a seven-day suspended committal imposed by Judge Corrie for breaching a residence order requiring return of his 12-year-old daughter to her mother by 4.00 pm on 25 March 2004.
The child refused to return; the judge found breach proved on the criminal standard because Mr M arrived at about 4.10 pm despite claiming he returned at 3.58 pm.
On 14 May counsel initially indicated two breaches were admitted, but the hearing proceeded on all allegations after confusion about what Mr M was admitting.
Judge Corrie imposed custody because Mr M could not pay a fine, having previously indicated imprisonment was inappropriate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a suspended committal order in ongoing children proceedings in the Oxford County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the finding of contempt stood but the suspended committal was discharged and no order substituted; detailed assessment of the respondent's Community Legal Services Funding costs.
enrichment.ratio: A suspended custodial committal requires that an immediate custodial sentence would first be justified, and imprisonment must not be imposed merely because the contemnor lacks means to pay a fine.
legal_issues: Whether procedural confusion on 14 May invalidated the committal hearing
Whether the judge was entitled to find breach of the return deadline proved
Whether a suspended seven-day committal was the appropriate penalty
Whether substituting no order was the correct appellate remedy

confidence.notes: Fact finding, sentencing error and final order are all clearly recorded in Ward LJ's judgment.

notes: Full Finelist director disqualification trial; cheque kiting unfitness findings and periods are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Finelist: director disqualification for cheque kiting at listed group
key_facts: The Secretary of State sought disqualification under section 6 against former Finelist Group directors after administrative receivers were appointed in October 2000 with substantial creditor deficiencies.
The group, formerly listed on the London Stock Exchange, operated an improper cheque kiting policy between AEW and Edmunds Walker bank accounts to create the illusion of banking covenant compliance.

Chairman and CEO Christopher Swan signed June cheques that cried out for enquiry; deputy chairman and audit committee chairman Brian North mishandled December 1999 whistleblowing allegations from COO Mr Reeve.
Finance director Reddy and executive director Ritchie gave disqualification undertakings; proceedings continued only against Swan and North.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of Secretary of State disqualification proceedings under section 6 of the 1986 Act against two remaining defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Both defendants held unfit; Swan disqualified for four years and North for three years under section 6.
enrichment.ratio: Signing high-value cheques implementing a group's cheque kiting policy without proper enquiry, or failing as audit committee chairman to pursue serious whistleblowing allegations with sufficient vigour, may fall so far below expected director competence as to constitute unfitness even without established dishonesty or actual loss.
legal_issues: Whether Swan knew or ought to have known of the group's cheque kiting policy
Whether North's handling of December 1999 allegations made him unfit
Whether cheque kiting without proved dishonesty or loss could support unfitness
What disqualification periods were appropriate under Re Sevenoaks Stationers categories
linked_authorities: Re Sevenoaks Stationers (Retail) Ltd
City Equitable Fire Insurance Company Ltd [1925] 1 Ch 407

notes: Short permission refusal on Turkish asylum; fact findings would support decision under any guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Tankisi: permission refused on Turkish asylum appeal
key_facts: Turkish citizen Tankisi claimed asylum based on family PKK sympathies, three detentions and maltreatment by police.
The adjudicator dismissed the appeal applying Polat country guidance; the IAT upheld the decision though Polat had been superseded.
The IAT found no personal interest in the appellant, with detentions linked to a school incident, a demonstration and his brother, and no recent authority interest over six years.
Sedley LJ had renewed the permission application in light of later IAT guidance in IK, but Carnwath LJ saw no arguable appeal ground.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed oral application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision upholding refusal of asylum.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no realistic prospect that the Court of Appeal would allow an appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where IAT fact findings show no continuing personal interest by the Turkish authorities, those findings would support refusal under any relevant country guidance and do not warrant permission to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT failed to apply updated country guidance after Polat
Whether fact findings on personal risk were sufficient to support refusal
Whether delay in lodging the permission application mattered
linked_authorities: Polat v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 04332

confidence.notes: Brief oral judgment with clear refusal and reasoning on facts and guidance.

notes: Consent order judicial review; magistrates accepted Wednesbury unreasonableness and convictions quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Anwar-Lindley: consent quashing of unsafe drink-driving convictions
key_facts: Fiona Anwar-Lindley was convicted at Reedley Magistrates' Court on 9 July 2004 of excess alcohol and careless driving.
She sought a case stated but magistrates refused, accepting their conviction was Wednesbury unreasonable and consenting to judicial review to quash it.
The magistrates had had no evidence that the claimant was driving on the relevant date.
Interested parties signed a consent order quashing the convictions, entering not guilty verdicts and awarding central funds costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with permission, of magistrates' refusal to state a case after driving convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Court made the consent order quashing convictions and entering not guilty verdicts with central funds costs, despite preferring a case stated route.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates accept a conviction was unreasonable and all parties consent to quashing with proper explanation, the Administrative Court may make a consent order rather than insist on a case stated, though a proper basis for quashing must be explained.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review was the proper route rather than a case stated
Whether to accept a consent order quashing convictions and entering not guilty verdicts
Importance of explaining the basis for quashing a public authority decision

notes: Litigant-in-person permission applications on possession and disrepair; detailed refusal reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Kush Housing: permission refused on possession and disrepair appeals
key_facts: Mr Lewis, a tenant at 252C Dalston Lane, appealed in person against a ground 8 possession order for rent arrears and dismissal of his disrepair claim against Kush Housing Association.

His Honour Judge Latham heard the disrepair trial and possession appeal together, preferring KHA's housing officer to Mr Lewis and finding he obstructed repairs while withholding housing benefit from the landlord.
Arrears exceeded eight weeks' rent at both the notice and hearing dates; the judge treated Mr Lewis as a tolerated trespasser from 31 March 2004.
Mr Lewis sought to adduce further evidence and raised Articles 6, 8 and 14 ECHR grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two Court of Appeal applications for permission to appeal (second appeal on possession) from HHJ Latham's combined judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Both permission applications dismissed, including ancillary disclosure and stay applications; no real prospect of success on fact findings or CPR 52.13 second appeal test.
enrichment.ratio: Findings that a tenant unreasonably blocked landlord repair attempts and failed to pass on housing benefit support dismissal of a disrepair claim; a ground 8 possession appeal by way of review fails where agreed counsel's note shows arrears above the statutory minimum.
legal_issues: Whether additional evidence satisfied Ladd v Marshall
Whether the district judge erred on ground 8 rent arrears
Whether disrepair damages could be set off against arrears
Whether the proposed second appeal raised a point of general principle under CPR 52.13
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

notes: Tax test case on depreciation in stock; Lightman J's section 74 analysis is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Mars UK: gross depreciation in stock must be added back for tax
key_facts: HM Inspector of Taxes appealed Special Commissioners' decision allowing Mars UK to subtract £3,039,000 depreciation capitalised in closing stock from the depreciation add-back in its 1996 tax computation.
Mars included manufacturing depreciation in stock valuation under UK GAAP and SSAP 9, charging net rather than gross depreciation in its profit and loss account.
The Revenue assessed additional tax of about £1.97 million, arguing section 74(1)(f) prohibited deducting any depreciation including amounts embedded in stock.
The case was a test case with a certificate for leapfrog appeal given its general importance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from Special Commissioners in a corporation tax test case on construction of section 74(1)(f).
enrichment.outcome: Revenue appeal allowed; depreciation included in stock must be added back with gross depreciation and section 74 overrides accountancy treatment.
enrichment.ratio: Section 74(1)(f) prohibits any deduction for depreciation in computing Schedule D Case I profits; capitalising depreciation in closing stock under GAAP does not prevent the full depreciation charge from being added back for tax purposes.
legal_issues: Whether stock figures represent cost or value for tax computation
Whether opening and closing stock should be treated as notional purchases and sales
Whether only net or gross depreciation was deducted in the accounts
Effect of Secan and Gallagher on the Commissioners' reasoning
linked_authorities: Gallagher v Jones [1993] STC 537
Secan Ltd v CIR 74 TC 1
Barclays Mercantile Business Finance Ltd v Mawson [2004] UKHL 51

notes: CCRC referral; murder quashed for defective provocation direction and Smith (Morgan) error.

enrichment.short_title: R v Farnell: murder quashed after defective provocation summing-up
key_facts: Mr Farnell killed neighbour Mr Pottage with a crowbar during a dispute over a barking puppy in May 1995 after a roadside argument.
He was convicted of murder at retrial in March 1996 having run diminished responsibility only; provocation was not pursued at trial though evidence existed.
Ognall J's summing-up treated provocation as effectively resolved against the defence because counsel had conceded no reasonable person would have reacted as Farnell did.
The CCRC referred the case after Divisional Court quashed its refusal to refer; fresh psychiatric evidence was not required for the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction following Criminal Cases Review Commission reference after earlier leave refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Murder conviction quashed as unsafe; manslaughter by provocation substituted with eight years' imprisonment; defendant's costs order for pre-legal aid work.
enrichment.ratio: A provocation direction that effectively removes the section 3 reasonable-man question from the jury is defective, and following R v Smith (Morgan) the jury must consider that test against relevant medical evidence; where both defects exist the conviction may not be safe.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's provocation direction complied with section 3 of the Homicide Act 1957
Whether R v Smith (Morgan) required the reasonable man test to reflect medical evidence
Whether the conviction remained safe despite trial counsel's concession
Appropriate sentence on substituted manslaughter by provocation
linked_authorities: R v Smith (Morgan) [2001] 1 AC 146
R v Josephine Smith [2002] EWCA Crim 261
R v Pendleton [2002] 1 WLR 72
R v Whitfield (1976) 63 Cr App R(S) 39

notes: Metallgesellschaft group litigation; compound interest for premature ACT period upheld on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Sempra Metals: compound interest on prematurely paid advance corporation tax
key_facts: Sempra Metals, a UK subsidiary of a German parent, paid advance corporation tax on dividends from 1974 to 1994 that could not be avoided because group income elections required both companies to be UK-resident.
The ECJ in Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst held the differential ACT treatment breached Community law and required full compensation for loss of use of money.
Park J held compensation for the premature tax payment period should be calculated using compound interest at a conventional borrower's rate; simple interest applied post-utilisation.
The Revenue appealed only against compound interest for the premature payment period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mr Justice Park's group litigation test-case order on quantum of ACT compensation under the Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst ruling.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed save for clarifying that compounding rests follow the periodic basis of the chosen rate; compound interest over the premature tax payment period upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Community law requires full compensation for premature ACT payments; where a conventional commercial borrowing rate is used, compound interest is necessary because such rates assume periodic payment or compounding and simple interest would under-compensate.
legal_issues: Whether compensation should be simple or compound interest over the premature payment period
Whether domestic section 35A simple-interest rules restrict the ECJ-mandated remedy
Whether category 1 and category 2 ACT claimants must be treated consistently
Relevance of Marshall (No 2) and Corus UK to the quantum question
linked_authorities: Metallgesellschaft Ltd v IRC (Cases C-397/98 and C-410/98)
Marshall v Southampton AHA (No 2) (Case C-271/91)
President of India v La Pintada Cia Navigacion SA [1985] AC 104
Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale v Islington LBC [1996] AC 669

notes: Case stated appeal on restraining order discharge; material change rule affirmed.

enrichment.short_title: Shaw v DPP: material change required to discharge restraining order
key_facts: Mr Shaw was convicted in 1999 of harassing his wife by letters and telephone calls from prison while serving sentences for rape offences.
A restraining order until further order prohibited contact; repeated discharge applications were dismissed in 1999, 2002 and 2003.
The fourth application in February 2004 was dismissed on 27 September 2004 with no material change since December 2003.
Shaw had threatened to reapply daily after an earlier refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated against a magistrates' court refusal to discharge a section 5(1) restraining order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; district judge was correct that a material change of circumstances is a primary consideration on repeat section 5(4) applications.
enrichment.ratio: On a further application to discharge a valid restraining order made until further order, the applicant must show a material change making continuation no longer necessary or appropriate; the court does not rehear the merits afresh without appeal.
legal_issues: Whether section 5(4) requires proof of material change of circumstances
Whether ex parte Davis bail principles apply to restraining orders
Whether successive applications must be determined on full merits with evidence each time
linked_authorities: Regina v Nottingham Justices, ex parte Davis [1980] 71 Cr App R 178

notes: Permission granted on Turkish asylum; IAT wrongly excluded A informer guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Civi: permission granted where IAT ignored informer country guidance
key_facts: Turkish citizen Civi claimed asylum based on military detention, torture and coercion to become an informer in December 2001, after which he fled.
The adjudicator accepted him as credible but dismissed the claim applying Polat guidance, finding only passive support and no current interest by authorities.
After High Court consent quashed refusal of IAT permission, the IAT upheld the adjudicator applying Polat and Subesh/Indrakumar limitations rather than A guidance on informers.
Family members in Turkey reported security force visits asking for his whereabouts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from an IAT decision upholding refusal of asylum after remittal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; arguable that the IAT wrongly confined itself to Polat and disregarded A guidance on informer status as a material risk factor.
enrichment.ratio: Where country guidance changes between adjudicator and IAT hearings, the tribunal may err by treating itself bound only by earlier Polat factors and excluding A guidance on coercion to become an informer as a material persecution risk factor.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT should have applied A country guidance rather than Polat alone
How Subesh and Indrakumar affect consideration of updated country guidance on fact appeals
Whether internal relocation to Istanbul was adequately reasoned
Whether recent visits to the appellant's family showed current interest by authorities
linked_authorities: Subesh v SSHD [2004] EWCA Civ 56
Indrakumar v SSHD [2003] EWCA Civ 1677
Polat v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKIAT 04332
